newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- What is on the Fed's mind?.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- What is on the Fed's mind?.

text.p: With most of the economic cards already on the table, U.S. credit market players are likely to spend next week trying to figure out how Federal Reserve officials interpreted the recently released data.

"There is no data next week that will be a dominant influence as far as what the Fed does on September 24 (when the bank's policy-setting arm meets next)," said Leonard Santow, managing director at Griggs and Santow Inc.
"What the market is going to concentrate on now is whatever speeches or talks any of the Federal Open Market Committee members give," Santow added.

Analysts said economic data released over the last few days dramatically reduced the odds of a Fed tightening in September. But still the scenario is mixed and what the Fed will do next seems to be anyone's guess at this point.

"I think everyone realizes it's going to be a close call as to what they'll do," Santow said. "People are trying to now figure out who's going to vote for what. That's really what the name of the game is going to be."
According to recent remarks, analysts said at least three voting members of the FOMC are perceived to be inclined to vote for a tightening of the monetary policy in September.
They are Gary Stern, head of the Minneapolis Fed, Robert McTeer, head of the Dallas Fed and Jerry Jordan, president of the Cleveland Fed.

The other two regional Fed heads, who are also current voting members of the FOMC, are William McDonough at the New York Fed and Edward Boehne at the Philadelphia Fed. Analysts said Boehne tends to be a centrist while McDonough is perceived to be more in line with Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan.
With that covered, analysts said the wild card tends to be the Fed governors, historically seen as being a little more on the "dovish" side.
Analysts said Federal Reserve Vice Chairwoman Alice Rivlin and Fed Governor Laurence Meyer are perceived in the market to be a little more keen to have a steady policy for now.

But they said recent remarks by Fed Governor Lawrence Lindsey suggested the official appears to be a little concerned about rapid economic growth and its consequences on inflation, which put him more on the "hawkish" side.
Analysts said recent data, which included producer and consumer price indices and retail sales, cut the odds of a Fed rate hike to between 40 and 50 percent from 65 percent.

August PPI on Thursday showed core inflation, excluding food and energy, dropped 0.1 percent. August core CPI issued Friday was up 0.1 percent and retail sales rose 0.2 percent last month against expectations of a 0.7 percent jump.

"One of the most important messages from ... the data is that it's now possible to contemplate a sub 2.0 percent GDP growth rate in the third quarter," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
"And we have to remember that back in late July people were worring that growth could be as high as 4.0 percent," Leahey said.

Among the data to be released next week, analysts said the market is likely to pay attention to the housing starts numbers for August and the Philadelphia Fed survey. Both are due out on September 19.
Also, the market will take in industrial production and capacity utilization for August on September 17.
"If anything will be important, that would be the housing and the Philly Fed," a money market trader said.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond rallied sharply on Friday to 1-18/32 at 97-17/32 in late trade. Its yield fell to 6.95 percent, the lowest level since August 23.
The Fed refrained from open market operations on Friday. The federal funds rate is seen opening at 5.38 percent on Monday, above the central bank's 5-1/4 percent target.
